scenes.name: Afrika Bambaataa y el electro-funk
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El instigador del electro-funk y del movimiento hip hop mundial, «una amenaza para el sistema»: DJ del Bronx con nombre zulú, líder de la Zulu Nation (breakdancers, grafiteros, DJ y MC). «Planet Rock» (Tommy Boy, 1982), con bajo atronador y sintetizadores espaciales, lanzó el sonido Tommy Boy (Jonzun Crew, Planet Patrol) e influyó en el house de Chicago, el bass de Miami y Egyptian Lover. Con «Renegades of Funk» (1983) mezcló cantos africanos y presentó a la Soul Sonic Force como superhéroes a lo Dr. Funkenstein; agradecía a Sly, Clinton, Bootsy y James Brown, con quien grabó «Unity» (1984) antes de que todos samplearan a Brown. Influyó en Jungle Brothers, Public Enemy, X-Clan o De La Soul. The Light (1988), con Clinton, Bootsy, Yellowman, UB40 y Boy George, era su visión de liberación global; Capitol lo recortó a un disco y fracasó. El padrino del hip hop.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: Malcolm McLaren y Bow Wow Wow
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Tras perder a los Sex Pistols, McLaren se exilia en París, descubre la música africana y, con la moda pirata del siglo XVIII de Vivienne Westwood, concibe su contraataque al postpunk «para universitarios»: ritmos burundeses (Simon Jeffes enseña polirritmia a Adam and the Ants, a quienes luego roba la banda), glamour, sexualidad adolescente y piratería en cassette. Con la anglobirmana Annabella Lwin, de catorce años, nace Bow Wow Wow: «C·30 C·60 C·90 Go!» (1980), Your Cassette Pet, solo en cassette con caja de cigarrillos, «W.O.R.K.» (el paro como liberación: «conviértanse en piratas»). Anticipa el walkman, la world music y la música como banda sonora portátil, pero también manipula y explota a sus músicos (la revista nunca editada Chicken, fotos con menores). See Jungle! (1982) es una obra maestra del pop justo cuando él pierde el interés; «I Want Candy» triunfa en Estados Unidos. Boy George pasa brevemente por el grupo antes de fundar Culture Club.

scenes.name: Segunda invasión británica y MTV
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En 1982 el new pop deja de ser un sueño de periodistas: «Don't You Want Me», «Tainted Love» y «The Look of Love» anuncian una nueva invasión, y en 1983 la segunda camada (Duran Duran, Culture Club, Wham!, Eurythmics, Thompson Twins) conquista Estados Unidos gracias a MTV, canal ideado por Michael Nesmith que, sin vídeos americanos, dependía de los británicos, más videogénicos y cultivados en el estilo («I want my MTV»). A Flock of Seagulls, Altered Images («Happy Birthday»), Simple Minds («Promised You a Miracle», New Gold Dream), Haircut 100, Kajagoogoo; Bowie se broncea con «Let's Dance». El new pop reexporta música negra (Chic, P-Funk, Quincy Jones) a la América blanca. En el Reino Unido, 1983 se vive en cambio como un año infausto: reelección de Thatcher, «Kill Ugly Pop» en las paredes y la vuelta de la conciencia social.

podcast.title: Blitz Club Origin
podcast.body: George O'Dowd, who later achieved international fame as Boy George, started his career working as a cloakroom attendant at London's Blitz Club. This club was a crucial gathering point for the fashion-forward Blitz kids in 1979 and 1980, serving as a cradle for the New Romantic movement. "And then there was the cloakroom attendant at the Blitz club. Some kid named George O'Dowd. He later became famous as Boy George."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Glam Connection to LGBT Community
podcast.body: Boy George, along with Culture Club, and Frankie Goes to Hollywood, represent the gay and non-binary club scene adjacent to the New Romantic movement, further extending glam's connection to the LGBT community and normalizing androgynous fashion. "especially people like Boy George, and Culture Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
podcast.body: Boy George of Culture Club openly stated that his life was profoundly changed by David Bowie's public comments in January 1972 about being gay. Bowie's statement gave him the courage to embrace and be true to his own identity. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nightclub Employee
podcast.body: Before his fame, Boy George worked at the coat check of one of the London nightclubs that were central to the rise of the New Romanticism movement. "Boy George used to work the code check at one of these clubs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Openly Gay Performer in New Wave
podcast.body: Boy George was one of the performers in the new wave scene who was, in fact, openly gay. His presence contributed to the genre's embrace of diverse sexual expressions and androgynous looks. "Some of these performers, such as Boy George, were in fact gay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Visuals in New Pop
podcast.body: Boy George, as part of Culture Club, embodied the visual aspect of New Pop, where artists' unique looks and music videos turned them into brief cultural phenomena in the early 80s. "Think Boy George and Culture Club, ABC in their Sharp Tuxedos, Orange Juice, a band of Scotland featuring Edwin Collins, Asda Camer was another, Heaven 17 was still another."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

xref.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
xref.body: Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood credited David Bowie's "coming out" statement in January 1972 as having changed his life. Bowie's public bravery gave Johnson the courage to be who he was. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for LGBTQ+ Individuals
xref.body: Bowie's public comments about his sexuality in 1972 struck a chord with thousands who were afraid to come out, giving them courage and a sense of shared identity with a famous figure. Figures like Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood have stated that Bowie's comments changed their lives. "Bowie gave them the courage to be who they were."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: MTV Prominence and Style
xref.body: Culture Club, fronted by Boy George and his unique look, was a British band that gained significant airtime on MTV, becoming a key part of the "second British invasion" that characterized the channel's early programming. "Culture Club with Boyd George's unique look..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominence in New Pop
xref.body: Culture Club, fronted by Boy George, was a prime example of a New Pop band. Their unique visual presentation, amplified by music videos, helped them become cultural phenomena in the early 1980s. "Think Boy George and Culture Club, ABC in their Sharp Tuxedos, Orange Juice, a band of Scotland featuring Edwin Collins, Asda Camer was another, Heaven 17 was still another."
